grh_6d1355809fc37f35e184.title: Magic Town
paragraphs: Public-opinion expert Rip Smith discovers that the small town of Grandview is a mathematical mirror of the entire United States: its population, politics, income, religion, and voting patterns match national averages almost perfectly. Facing failure in his polling business, Rip secretly moves in as an insurance man and uses Grandview as a shortcut for national surveys. He also falls for local newspaper editor Mary Peterman, who is fighting for civic improvements and initially believes Rip has joined the town in good faith. Once his secret is exposed, national publicity turns Grandviewâ€™s status into a commercial craze, and the townspeople begin selling their opinions as if they were infallible. Their first self-conscious poll is spectacularly wrong, the boom collapses, and the town is humiliated. Rip then asks one final question: what does the average American do after making a mistake? Grandview answers by rebuilding together, proving its value not as a magic oracle but as a community capable of correcting itself, while Rip and Mary reconcile.

This [[show|screen-directors-playhouse|Screen Directors Playhouse]] broadcast aired on January 6, 1950. It is listed as episode 50 in the archive. [[org|org.f2f0561f0ce2ddc5|NBC Radio Network]] carried the broadcast. The cast includes Edward Marr, George Marshall, Hans Conried, Jerry Hausner, and Jimmy Stewart. Other credited names include Jimmy Wallington as announcer.
The surviving recording runs about 30 minutes. The broadcast is also associated with [[org|org.47c43e9eb0213c63|RCA]].
This version presents a radio version of [[work|work.sdp.film.4e33e6a6cc196b53|Magic Town]].

grh_6d31b6f5d8039090c0a9.title: Cluny Brown
paragraphs: Free-spirited Cluny Brown has an inconvenient passion for plumbing that her uncle considers improper for a young woman, and she is sent into domestic service at an English country estate to learn her place. There she meets refugee professor Adam Belinski, another outsider who recognizes how badly Cluny fits the rigid social rules around her. Cluny tries to become respectable by accepting the attentions of conventional pharmacist Mr. Wilson, but her impulse to repair the plumbing during his mother's formal party proves that she cannot turn herself into the woman he expects. Wilson recoils, while Belinski offers Cluny a life where her impulses are part of who she is rather than a disgrace. She leaves with him, becoming Mrs. Belinski and trading a prescribed place in society for an uncertain but shared future.

grh_6d872b6369fd194e84c0.title: The Hoofer
paragraphs: Successful dancer Evangeline Moore returns to Rivers End exhausted and refuses ever to dance again. Years earlier she and her partner and fiancé Johnny 'Skeeter' Briggs were on the verge of a major stage break when he was inducted into the Army. Evangeline later toured for servicemen with the USO, but after Johnny's letters stopped she became convinced he was dead and finally collapsed into grief and self-pity. Dr. Christian traces Johnny and learns that he survived the war with a disabling injury. Believing Evangeline should not be tied to a helpless man, Johnny deliberately stayed silent while undergoing months of rehabilitation and dance practice. Dr. Christian arranges for Evangeline to attend a wounded-soldiers hospital show where Johnny makes his first public dancing appearance since his injury. The two reunite, discover that neither has stopped loving the other, and decide to dance together again.

The cast includes Jean Hersholt and Rosemary De Camp. Other credited names include Art Gilmore as announcer.
The surviving recording runs about 25 minutes. The broadcast is also associated with [[org|org.b199d95f77b6c241|Vaseline]].

grh_6debd522efad47592213.title: The Lady Eve
paragraphs: Cardsharp Jean Harrington falls for wealthy, naive snake expert Charles Pike aboard ship, but he rejects her when he discovers she has been working a con with her father. Determined to get even, Jean reinvents herself as the aristocratic Lady Eve Sidwich and returns to Charles's life under an assumed identity, making him fall for her a second time. grh_6dd67efa061d0cfcfb8e.title: War Criminals and Punishment
paragraphs: A policy-driven dramatization of George Creel's War Criminals and Punishment argues that Axis leaders must not escape accountability after the war. Using historical examples from the aftermath of World War I, staged voices outline ways German leaders previously avoided punishment and warn against repeating those failures. The program calls for unconditional surrender, military occupation and disarmament, prosecution of war criminals and the destruction of Prussian militarism as necessary steps toward a durable peace.
